title: Preventing migraine: a CGRP antibody
description: CGRP is a signalling molecule involved in migraine. Antibodies against it, given as an injection under the skin, are a newer way of preventing attacks. One study scanned people with migraine while a painful stimulus (ammonia gas puffed into one nostril) was applied, before and two to three weeks after a first injection of galcanezumab. Afterwards, the hypothalamus and parts of the cerebellum responded less on average. In this episode brightness shows the change since before treatment: violet means less than before.
caveat: All findings come from one study of 26 people with migraine, without a comparison group of people without migraine. Some had a headache on one or both scan days. The larger reduction in people whose migraines improved, meaning 30% fewer headache days after three months, comes from a subgroup of 15 who had the same headache state at both scans. A related antibody that blocks the CGRP receptor instead (erenumab) acted on a different network in an earlier study, so the brain effect depends on the antibody. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

phases.name: What changed
phases.caption: During the same painful test, the hypothalamus and parts of the cerebellum respond less than before the injection, on average across all 26 people. In a subgroup, the hypothalamus reduction was larger in people whose migraines improved.
